lessons.title: The Language of ESOPs: Grant, Vesting, Exercise Price and Expiry

children.text: A grant letter is a one-page document that decides how much money you eventually make. It is also written in a language nobody teaches you. This lesson takes that language apart, term by term, using a single grant you can follow from the first day to the last.
The grant.

Ritika joins a health-tech startup in Hyderabad on 1 April 2026. Her letter says: 4,800 options, exercise price ₹18, vesting over 48 months with a 12-month cliff, 25% at the cliff and the rest monthly, exercisable up to 5 years after vesting.

body.text: Granted is a promise. Vested is what you have earned. Exercised is what you actually own. Three different words, three very different amounts of money.

children.text: Two of these are fixed forever on the
grant date
: the number of options and the
exercise price
. Everything else is a clock that starts ticking.

markDefs.definition: The date the board approves your options. Your exercise price and the start of your vesting clock are both fixed on this date.
The fixed price per share you pay to convert a vested option into a share. Also called the strike price or grant price.

children.text: Vesting: Earning What You Were Promised
Vesting

is the company saying: stay, and this becomes yours in instalments. Indian law sets a floor here. Under Rule 12(6)(a) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, there must be a minimum of one year between the grant of options and vesting. Listed companies face the same one-year minimum under SEBI’s SBEB and Sweat Equity Regulations, 2021. Both frameworks waive it if an employee dies or suffers permanent incapacity while in employment, in which case the options vest immediately, with the legal heirs or nominees in the case of death.

markDefs.definition: The process of earning the right to exercise your options, usually in instalments over three to four years of continued employment.

body.label: Minimum gap between grant and vesting in India
body.context: Rule 12(6)(a) for unlisted companies and the SEBI SBEB Regulations, 2021 for listed ones. Relaxed only on death or permanent incapacity.

children.text: The cliff
A
cliff

is the harshest term in the letter, and the most common. For 12 months Ritika vests nothing at all. On 1 April 2027 she vests 1,200 options in a single step, which is 25% of her grant. From month 13 onward, 100 options vest every month for the remaining 36 months.

markDefs.definition: An initial period, most often one year, during which nothing vests at all. Complete it and the first chunk vests in one go. Leave before it and you get nothing.

body.text: If Ritika resigns on day 360, two weeks before her cliff, she leaves with zero options. Not a pro-rated share, not a goodwill gesture. Zero. Check your cliff date before you sign a resignation letter.

body.title: Ritika’s cumulative vested options over 48 months

children.text: The line is flat for a year, jumps at the cliff, then climbs steadily. That shape is the whole retention strategy in one picture: the longer she stays, the more she leaves behind by quitting.

body.title: How Much Has She Earned?
body.prompt: Ritika is 30 months into her 48-month schedule. With 25% (1,200 options) vesting at the 12-month cliff and 100 options vesting every month after that, how many of her 4,800 options have vested?
body.explanation: At the cliff she vested 1,200. From month 13 to month 30 is 18 months, so 18 × 100 = 1,800 more. Total vested = 3,000 options, leaving 1,800 unvested.

columns.label: Vested
points: Earned. You may exercise them, subject to the scheme rules
Survive your resignation, but usually only for a short exercise window
Can be converted into real shares by paying the exercise price
Count when you value your holding

columns.label: Unvested

Almost always forfeited the day you leave
Cannot be exercised at any price
Should be treated as zero in any offer comparison

children.text: Exercise Price: What You Pay, and the Legal Floor
Ritika pays
per share whenever she exercises, however valuable the share has become. Indian companies have wide freedom to set this price, with one hard rule: it cannot be below the
face value
of the share. Startups usually set it at or near face value so employees can afford to exercise. Listed companies set it by a formula approved by shareholders, and must disclose it.

markDefs.definition: The nominal value of a share as stated in the company’s capital structure, such as ₹1 or ₹10. It is the legal floor for an ESOP exercise price.

children.text: Do not confuse the exercise price with the
fair market value

. The exercise price is frozen on the grant date. The fair market value moves. If the company’s shares are valued at ₹250 when Ritika exercises her 3,000 vested options, she pays ₹54,000 and receives shares valued at ₹7,50,000. The gap of ₹6,96,000 is her gain, and it is exactly what the taxman looks at. Chapter 4 covers that.

markDefs.definition: Fair Market Value: the value of one share on a given date. For listed shares it comes from the exchange. For unlisted companies it comes from a valuation report.

body.caption: Ritika needs 3,000 × ₹18 = ₹54,000 in hand, before any tax on the gain.

body.text: A low exercise price is not generosity, it is practicality. If a startup sets the exercise price at the latest round valuation, employees may simply be unable to fund the cheque, and the whole plan becomes decoration.

body.title: The Cheque She Must Write
body.prompt: If Ritika waits until all 4,800 options have vested and exercises the entire grant at ₹18 per share, how much cash does she need to pay the company?
body.explanation: 4,800 × ₹18 = ₹86,400. This is money out of her pocket, separate from any tax due on the gain. Planning for this cash outflow is a real part of ESOP planning.

children.text: Exercise Period and Expiry: The Deadline Nobody Reads
Vesting gives you the right. The
exercise period
tells you how long that right lasts. Ritika can exercise each vested tranche for 5 years after it vests. After that comes
expiry
: the option simply dies.

markDefs.definition: The window during which you are allowed to exercise vested options. Miss it and the options lapse.
The last date on which an option can be exercised. After it, the option is dead and worth nothing, however valuable the share has become.

body.title: Four dates, and why each one matters

children.text: Grant date: fixes your exercise price and starts your vesting clock. Nothing is taxed here.
Vesting date: you earn the right to exercise. Still no tax, and still no shares.
Exercise date: you pay the exercise price and receive shares. This is the first tax event, on the gap between fair market value and what you paid.
Sale date: you sell the shares. The change in value since exercise is a capital gain or loss. Chapter 4 works through both events with numbers.

body.title: When Does the Value Disappear?
body.question: Ritika’s first tranche vested on 1 April 2027 with a five-year exercise period. She never exercises it. On 1 June 2032 the company lists and the share touches ₹900. What are those 1,200 options worth to her?
options: ₹10,58,400, because the shares are worth far more than her exercise price
Nothing, because the tranche expired on 1 April 2032
She can still exercise within 30 days of listing
The company must compensate her in cash
body.explanation: An expired option is dead. The exercise period is a hard deadline, and a listing afterwards does not revive it. Diarise your expiry dates the day you receive a grant letter.

body.title: The Legal Minimum
body.textWithBlank: Indian rules require a minimum gap of ___ year between the grant of options and the date they vest.
body.explanation: Rule 12(6)(a) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 for unlisted companies, mirrored by the SEBI SBEB and Sweat Equity Regulations, 2021 for listed ones. It is waived on death or permanent incapacity.

body.title: Reading the Letter Properly
body.scenario: Vikram, an operations manager in Indore, receives a grant letter: 6,000 options, exercise price ₹10, vesting 25% each year over four years, exercise period 90 days after each vesting date. He is delighted and signs immediately.
body.prompt: What has Vikram missed, and what should he do about it?
body.modelAnswer: The exercise period is the problem. A 90-day window after each vesting date means he must pay ₹15,000 for each 1,500-option tranche within three months of it vesting, or lose it, even though the company is unlisted and he cannot sell the shares to fund the payment. He will be putting real money into an illiquid asset four times over, and paying perquisite tax at each exercise. Before signing he should ask whether the exercise period can run until a liquidity event or for several years after vesting, which is the more common structure. He should also ask what happens to the window if he resigns, and get the company’s latest fair market value so he can size the tax hit at each exercise.

children.text: Words Companies Add, and What They Usually Mean
Performance vesting:
options vest only if targets are met, not just with time. Ask exactly how the target is measured and who decides.
Acceleration:
vesting speeds up if the company is acquired. Very valuable, and less common in Indian grants than employees assume.
Lock-in:
a period after exercise during which you cannot sell the shares.
Buyback discretion:
the company may, but need not, repurchase your shares. Read this as no guarantee of liquidity.

Earning the right to exercise, in instalments, usually over three to four years.
The initial period, typically one year, in which nothing vests at all.
The fixed amount you pay per share. It cannot be below the face value of the share.
The window in which vested options may be exercised, after which they lapse.
The date an option dies. After it, the option is worthless whatever the share is worth.

points: Granted, vested and exercised mean three different things. Only exercised options make you a shareholder.
The grant date fixes your exercise price and the number of options. Everything else is a clock.
Indian rules require at least one year between grant and vesting, waived only on death or permanent incapacity.
A cliff is all or nothing. Leaving one day before it means leaving with zero.
The exercise price cannot be below the face value of the share, and it stays frozen even as the fair market value moves.
Exercising costs real cash: vested options multiplied by the exercise price, before any tax.
Options expire. Note every expiry date from the day you receive the grant letter.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Grant terms differ from company to company, and the figures used here are illustrative. Read your own grant letter and scheme document, and consult a qualified professional.
